quiz_questions.question_text: Neha’s friend asks how she is. She says “Fine”, but she has felt low and restless all day. Based on this tutorial, what is the most helpful first step for Neha?

options.text: Pause and notice what she is actually feeling, and try to name it
Keep saying “fine” so she does not bother anyone
Distract herself until the feeling goes away
Decide that feeling low means something is wrong with her

quiz_questions.explanation: Noticing and naming what we feel is the first step to understanding what the emotion is telling us.

quiz_questions.question_text: Rajesh feels nervous the night before his driving test. Which way of seeing his nervousness fits this course best?

options.text: It is a weakness he should hide
It shows he will probably fail
It is a bad emotion he should stop feeling
It is a signal that the test matters to him

quiz_questions.explanation: Emotions are neither good nor bad. They are signals about how we are experiencing a situation.

quiz_questions.question_text: Before an important meeting, Asif notices that his jaw is tight and his stomach is churning, even before he knows what he is feeling. How is his emotion showing up?

options.text: In his thoughts
In his actions
In his body
It is not an emotion

quiz_questions.explanation: Emotions show up in our thoughts, body and feelings. Often the body reacts first, before we can name the feeling.

quiz_questions.question_text: Kavitha feels angry when her cousin takes her scooter without asking. According to this course, how should she understand her anger?

options.text: As a bad emotion she must push away
As a signal that something feels unfair to her, which can help her decide what to do
As proof that her cousin is a bad person
As a reason to shout at her cousin straight away

quiz_questions.explanation: Anger points to something that feels unfair. Listening to that message helps her respond calmly, for example by asking her cousin to check with her first.

quiz_questions.question_text: Lokesh is trying to describe how he feels after a friend cancels their plans. Which description will help him most?

options.text: “I feel bad.”
“I don’t have any feelings about it.”
“Whatever.”
“I feel disappointed and a bit left out.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Naming feelings precisely, such as “disappointed” rather than just “bad”, helps us understand what we need and how to respond.

quiz_questions.question_text: Just before her class presentation, Priyanka’s heart is racing and her stomach feels upset. What is the best explanation?

options.text: She is getting ill and should go home
She is not suited to presenting
Her body is getting ready for action because the presentation matters to her
Something is seriously wrong with her

quiz_questions.explanation: A racing heart and an upset stomach are part of the body’s normal fear response. They are signs of preparation, not of failure.

quiz_questions.question_text: Tarun needs to call his bank about a wrong charge, but he has been putting it off for three weeks because he dreads the conversation. Which fear reaction is this?

options.text: Run
Freeze
Fight
Prepare

quiz_questions.explanation: Avoiding or putting things off is the modern form of running away. It keeps the fear alive, because nothing changes.

quiz_questions.question_text: Nisha’s heart is pounding as she waits outside the interview room. What could she tell herself that would help her most?

options.text: “I must calm down completely before I go in.”
“My body is excited because this matters to me. Let me use that energy.”
“I’m nervous, so I’ll probably mess this up.”
“I shouldn’t be feeling anything at all.”

quiz_questions.explanation: It is hard to switch off a racing heart. Seeing it as excitement and energy for the task is more helpful than fighting it.

quiz_questions.question_text: During his viva, Deepak suddenly cannot remember anything, even though he knows the topic well. Which fear reaction is this?

options.text: Excitement
Run
Fight
Freeze

quiz_questions.explanation: A mind going blank under pressure is the modern form of the “freeze” reaction.

quiz_questions.question_text: Ritu is scared of her first swimming class. Which approach is most likely to help her?

options.text: Start with small steps, such as standing in the shallow end, and tell a friend how she feels
Tell herself she is silly for being afraid
Skip the class until the fear goes away on its own
Jump into the deep end to get it over with

quiz_questions.explanation: Breaking a fear into small steps and sharing it with someone supportive makes it easier to face.

quiz_questions.question_text: A colleague makes fun of Suresh’s work in a meeting. Suresh’s face goes hot and his fists clench. What is the most helpful thing for him to do first?

options.text: Reply immediately so the colleague knows he cannot get away with it
Leave the meeting and avoid the colleague for a week
Pretend he feels nothing
Notice his body’s alarm and pause before he responds

quiz_questions.explanation: A hot face and clenched fists are early warning signs of anger. Noticing them gives him a few seconds to choose how to respond.

quiz_questions.question_text: For weeks, Pooja has felt left out because her roommate keeps going out with other friends. One evening she snaps, “You don’t care about me at all!” What is most likely underneath her anger?

options.text: Jealousy of her roommate’s clothes
Hurt and loneliness that she has kept to herself
Tiredness from studying
Nothing; she is simply an angry person

quiz_questions.explanation: Anger is often the feeling we show, while hurt or fear is the feeling we hide.

quiz_questions.question_text: After an argument with his brother, Arjun decides to punch a pillow while replaying the argument in his head, to “get the anger out”. What is the likely result?

options.text: His anger is likely to stay strong, or grow
His anger will disappear quickly
He will feel happy afterwards
He will forget the argument

quiz_questions.explanation: Venting while focusing on the person who angered us tends to keep anger going. Pausing quietly or stepping back helps more.

quiz_questions.question_text: Karthik is furious because his friend has cancelled their plans for the third time. Which of these is an example of “stepping back”?

options.text: Replaying the cancellations in his head all evening
Sending an angry message straight away
Picturing the situation as if he were watching it happen to someone else
Telling himself he should not feel angry

quiz_questions.explanation: Looking at the situation from the outside, like a fly on the wall, helps anger cool down and makes it easier to think clearly.

quiz_questions.question_text: Divya is angry that her sister read her diary. Which response expresses her anger without causing harm?

options.text: “You’re the worst sister in the world.”
“I felt hurt and embarrassed when you read my diary. Please don’t do it again.”
Saying nothing and refusing to speak to her for a month
Reading her sister’s messages to get back at her

quiz_questions.explanation: Speaking about the hurt, not attacking the person, lets anger do its job: pointing out something unfair so it can change.

quiz_questions.question_text: Lavanya feels sad after her best friend moves to another city for work. Based on this reading, what is her sadness most likely asking her to do?

options.text: Forget about the friendship
Stay connected and reach out for support
Hide the feeling so she does not seem weak
Make new friends immediately so she stops feeling sad

quiz_questions.explanation: Sadness tells us we have lost something we value, and it pushes us to seek comfort and stay connected.

quiz_questions.question_text: Raghav has felt low most of the day, nearly every day, for three weeks. He has lost interest in cricket and his friends, and he is sleeping badly. What is the best step?

options.text: Wait a few more months; it is probably normal sadness
Keep it to himself so he does not worry anyone
Stay busy so he does not think about it
Talk to a counsellor, doctor or trusted adult

quiz_questions.explanation: Low mood and loss of interest that last two weeks or more can be signs of depression, which needs support from a professional.

quiz_questions.question_text: Every day, a new classmate eats alone in the canteen and looks low. What is the most helpful thing to do?

options.text: Leave them alone; it is not your business
Tell others that the new student seems strange
Sit with them, ask if they are okay and invite them to join your group
Wait for a teacher to notice

quiz_questions.explanation: A small act of care, like the one Gopi showed Raja in the tutorial, can make someone’s sadness much lighter.

quiz_questions.question_text: Sameer feels sad for a few days after failing an exam. Then he starts to plan how he will prepare better next time. How would you describe what he went through?

options.text: Normal sadness that eased with time and helped him think about what matters
Depression that needs urgent treatment
A sign of weakness
Something he should have hidden from everyone

quiz_questions.explanation: Normal sadness follows a loss or disappointment and eases with time. Depression lasts longer and affects most areas of life.

quiz_questions.question_text: Nandini is going through a hard time, but she tells everyone “I’m okay” because she does not want to be a burden. What is the most likely result?

options.text: The sadness will pass faster
Hiding sadness makes people stronger
Her friends will feel burdened if she shares
The sadness may feel heavier and last longer than if she shared it

quiz_questions.explanation: Sadness that is shared usually passes sooner than sadness that is hidden. Reaching out is what sadness is asking for.

quiz_questions.question_text: Karan saved for a year to buy a new motorbike. He was thrilled at first, but after two weeks it felt ordinary. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Short bursts of pleasure from new things fade as we get used to them
He bought the wrong bike
He is an ungrateful person
Happiness never lasts for anyone

quiz_questions.explanation: New purchases bring real joy, but we soon get used to them. Deeper happiness comes from sources that build slowly.

quiz_questions.question_text: Which of these is most likely to bring Asha lasting happiness?

options.text: Buying the latest phone
Getting many likes on a photo
Spending regular, unhurried time with close friends and family
Watching funny videos every evening

quiz_questions.explanation: Close relationships are among the strongest sources of long-term happiness. The other options give short bursts of pleasure.

quiz_questions.question_text: Priya worries that something is wrong with her because she does not feel happy every single day. What does this reading suggest?

options.text: She should keep buying things until she feels happy again
Happy people feel good all the time
She should hide how she feels so others do not worry
Happiness comes and goes like every emotion, and expecting to feel happy all the time makes ordinary days feel like failures

quiz_questions.explanation: Like every emotion, happiness comes and goes. An ordinary or flat day is normal, not a sign that something is wrong.

quiz_questions.question_text: Mohan wants to feel more positive about his life over the next few months. Which habit is most likely to help?

options.text: Buying something expensive he has wanted for a long time
Writing down a few things he is grateful for each week
Working longer hours to earn more
Spending more time scrolling social media

quiz_questions.explanation: Regularly noticing what we are grateful for helps people feel more positive about their lives.

quiz_questions.question_text: Imran gets admission to the college he dreamed of. He wonders whether to tell his friends or keep it quiet. What does this tutorial suggest?

options.text: Keep it quiet so others do not feel jealous
Only tell people who can help his career
Share it; sharing good news makes the joy grow and strengthens bonds
It does not matter either way

quiz_questions.explanation: Like Sneha in the tutorial, sharing happiness spreads it to others and brings people closer.

quiz_questions.question_text: Aditi forgot her close friend’s birthday. Which thought shows healthy guilt?

options.text: “I’m a terrible friend. Nobody should trust me.”
“It’s her fault for not reminding me.”
“It doesn’t matter; she’ll get over it.”
“I forgot her birthday. I should apologise and make it up to her.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Guilt focuses on a specific action and pushes us to repair it. “I’m a terrible friend” is shame, which is about the whole self.

quiz_questions.question_text: Meena borrowed her classmate’s notes before an exam and spilled tea on them. She feels guilty about it. Which response shows her guilt being helpful?

options.text: She keeps thinking about it for days and avoids her classmate.
She tells her classmate what happened, says sorry, and offers to photocopy a clean set from a friend.
She tells herself it does not matter, because the notes were old anyway.
She returns the notes quietly and hopes her classmate does not notice.

quiz_questions.explanation: Guilt is helpful when it pushes us to put things right. A shows guilt that keeps going but leads nowhere. C pushes the feeling away with an excuse, and D tries to hide the mistake.

quiz_questions.question_text: Kabir borrowed his roommate’s phone charger and lost it. Which apology is most likely to rebuild trust?

options.text: “Sorry about the charger, but you did leave it lying around.”
“Sorry, I lost your charger. I’ve ordered a new one; it comes on Thursday.”
“I’m so sorry. I’m terrible with things. I feel awful about it.”
“Sorry if you’re upset. It’s only a charger, though.”

quiz_questions.explanation: A sincere apology admits what happened and offers to make it right. A blames the roommate, and D makes the loss seem small. C sounds sorry, but it is about Kabir’s feelings instead of fixing the problem.

quiz_questions.question_text: Months after apologising for a small mistake, Tanvi still lies awake blaming herself for it every night. What does this reading suggest?

options.text: This is healthy guilt; she should keep thinking about it
Her guilt has turned into constant self-blame, which does not help; talking to someone she trusts or a counsellor could help
She should apologise again every day
She should stop caring about anyone’s feelings

quiz_questions.explanation: Guilt is useful when it leads to repair. Once we have tried to make things right, endless self-blame only harms us.

quiz_questions.question_text: Varun said something hurtful to a friend and feels guilty. Which approach is most likely to help him repair the friendship?

options.text: Being understanding towards himself while taking responsibility for what he did
Pretending it did not happen
Telling himself he is a horrible person
Waiting for his friend to bring it up

quiz_questions.explanation: People who treat themselves with kindness after a mistake find it easier to face what they did and put it right.

quiz_questions.question_text: Anjana feels jealous when her classmate wins a scholarship. Which question would help her most?

options.text: “Why does everything go right for her?”
“What does this jealousy show me that I want for myself?”
“How can I stop her getting the next one?”
“Why am I always unlucky?”

quiz_questions.explanation: Jealousy points to something we want or value. Asking what it is pointing to turns the feeling into useful information.

quiz_questions.question_text: Rohan feels jealous when his colleague is promoted. Then he learns she spent months learning new software in her own time. What is this most likely to do?

options.text: Make his jealousy stronger
Prove the promotion was unfair
Help his jealousy turn into admiration, and show him what is possible with effort
Make no difference

quiz_questions.explanation: Seeing the effort behind someone’s success makes it feel earned, and possible for us too, just as Rohit saw Vikram practising in the tutorial.

quiz_questions.question_text: Swati’s colleague gets a promotion that Swati had hoped for. Which response shows jealousy turning into admiration and growth?

options.text: Congratulating her, asking what helped her prepare and picking one skill to work on
Telling others the promotion was unfair
Refusing to congratulate her
Deciding she will never be promoted

quiz_questions.explanation: Admiration turns energy forward: learning from the other person and taking a small step.

quiz_questions.question_text: Every night, Bharat spends an hour scrolling through photos of his friends’ trips and new jobs, and goes to bed feeling worse about his own life. What change is most likely to help?

options.text: Scrolling for longer until he feels better
Deleting all his friends
Posting more photos to compete
Scrolling less, and messaging or meeting friends instead

quiz_questions.explanation: Passively scrolling through others’ best moments tends to increase envy. Actively connecting with friends does not have this effect.

quiz_questions.question_text: Meena feels jealous because her cousin’s parents can afford to send her abroad to study, and her own family cannot. According to the tutorial, what is this jealousy most likely asking her to do?

options.text: Compete harder with her cousin
Ignore the feeling completely
Stop speaking to her cousin
Notice the need underneath, such as wanting a good education, and look for a healthy way to meet it

quiz_questions.explanation: When jealousy points to something we cannot change, it is asking us to notice an unmet need, not to compare. quiz_questions.question_text: Kiran describes her morning journey to her mother. Which of her statements is a statement of reality?

options.text: “The bus was annoyingly slow.”
“The bus left the stop at 8:10 am.”
“The journey was boring.”
“Buses are so uncomfortable.”

quiz_questions.explanation: “The bus left at 8:10 am” can be checked. The others describe how Kiran experienced the journey.

quiz_questions.question_text: Sneh’s teacher returns her essay with many corrections in red. Sneh’s first thought is, “She thinks I’m a bad writer.” Which thought would most likely help Sneh feel better without ignoring the facts?

options.text: “She took the time to show me how to improve.”
“The corrections don’t matter. My essay was fine.”
“Other students probably got even more corrections.”
“I’ll just stop trying hard on essays.”

quiz_questions.explanation: The corrections are the reality, and Sneh can’t change them. But she can change how she interprets them. B ignores the facts, C compares her with others, and D gives up. A sees the same corrections in a more helpful way.

quiz_questions.question_text: Sita and Varun both score 75% in an exam. Sita is delighted; Varun is upset. What best explains the difference?

options.text: One of them has misread their marks
Varun is an unhappy person
A score of 75% always causes mixed feelings
They interpret the same score differently, so they feel different emotions

quiz_questions.explanation: Reality alone does not create emotions. How each of them interprets the score does.

quiz_questions.question_text: Harish’s friend has not replied to his message for a day. Harish thinks, “She is ignoring me,” and feels hurt. What kind of thought is “She is ignoring me”?

options.text: Reality, because she has not replied
A fact he has checked
An interpretation; she may be busy, unwell or without her phone
A belief that cannot be changed

quiz_questions.explanation: “She has not replied for a day” is reality. “She is ignoring me” is Harish’s guess about why.

quiz_questions.question_text: Two friends watch the same cricket match, one supporting each team. They argue about an umpire’s decision, and each is sure they saw it correctly. What best explains this?

options.text: The team each supports shapes how they interpret what they see
One of them has poor eyesight
The television showed different things
There is always one correct interpretation

quiz_questions.explanation: Our loyalties and past experiences shape our interpretations, so the same event can look very different to two people.

quiz_questions.question_text: Arun believes, “If I don’t top every exam, I’m a failure.” He feels anxious all the time, he is exhausted, and his family keeps telling him he is too hard on himself. What should Arun do?

options.text: Check this belief, because he is getting unwanted results, unwanted feedback and repeated negative emotions
Keep the belief, because it pushes him to work hard
Ignore his family, because they do not understand
Study even harder until the anxiety goes away

quiz_questions.explanation: All three warning signs are present, so the belief needs checking. It may have helped him once, but it is no longer effective.

quiz_questions.question_text: Deepa decides her new neighbour is unfriendly because he did not smile when they first met. Later she learns he is very shy. What shaped her first interpretation?

options.text: The facts of the situation
Her neighbour’s personality
Bad luck
Her belief that friendly people always smile

quiz_questions.explanation: Beliefs work like lenses. Deepa’s belief about smiling shaped how she interpreted his behaviour.

quiz_questions.question_text: Kavitha believes she must reply to every message immediately, or people will think she is rude. She is always stressed and cannot focus on her studies. What does this suggest?

options.text: Her belief is wrong, and she should feel bad about it
She should reply even faster
Her belief may be ineffective, because it is bringing results and emotions she does not want
Beliefs cannot affect focus

quiz_questions.explanation: The belief is not right or wrong, but it is not working for her. Repeated stress and poor results are signs that it needs checking.

quiz_questions.question_text: Mahesh’s teammate replies late to a message about their project, and Mahesh feels irritated. Which belief would most likely leave him feeling calm instead?

options.text: “Good teammates always reply quickly.”
“Nobody takes this project seriously except me.”
“People have busy lives, and a late reply doesn’t mean they don’t care.”
“I should do everything myself.”

quiz_questions.explanation: The same reality can lead to different feelings depending on the belief we see it through.

quiz_questions.question_text: Fatima believes that students who ask questions in class are just showing off. She has heard her older cousins say this for years. Where did her belief most likely come from?

options.text: What she has heard from people around her
Scientific evidence
Her own experience of asking questions
Her teachers’ advice

quiz_questions.explanation: Many beliefs come from what we hear from family, friends and society. Once we notice where a belief came from, we can ask whether it still helps us.

quiz_questions.question_text: Shreya believes, “I can’t speak up in meetings.” She wants to change this belief. What is the first step?

options.text: Volunteer to give the next big presentation
Notice the belief and write it down in plain words
Tell herself she is the best speaker in the office
Avoid meetings until she feels confident

quiz_questions.explanation: We cannot change a belief until we notice it. The steps are: become aware, check it, create a new belief, practise, write down progress and celebrate.

quiz_questions.question_text: A week after starting to work on a new belief, Ganesh still feels nervous and uncomfortable each time he practises. What does this reading suggest?

options.text: This is normal; changing a belief takes time, and discomfort is part of the journey
The new belief is wrong, and he should give up
He should wait until he feels confident before practising again
Beliefs can never really change

quiz_questions.explanation: Like Tara in the tutorial, people’s emotions shift slowly, from fear and discomfort to relief and pride.

quiz_questions.question_text: Leela wants to believe, “I can learn to swim.” Which experience is most likely to strengthen this belief?

options.text: Reading that some people are natural swimmers
Being told she is too old to learn
Watching a friend who could not swim last year now swimming confidently, and managing one width of the pool herself
Thinking about swimming without getting into the water

quiz_questions.explanation: Seeing someone like us succeed, and having small successes of our own, are among the strongest ways to build belief in what we can do.

quiz_questions.question_text: Neel believes, “I’m hopeless at cooking.” Which is the most helpful new belief and first action?

options.text: “I’m a master chef”; cook a feast for twenty guests this weekend
“Cooking doesn’t matter”; keep ordering food
“I’ll never learn”; accept it
“With practice, I can learn a few simple dishes”; cook one dish this week and note how it went

quiz_questions.explanation: A helpful new belief is believable, and small actions, written down, help it grow stronger.

quiz_questions.question_text: Imran is working on a new belief and wants to keep track of his progress. Which approach is likely to help most?

options.text: Keeping a rough idea in his head
Writing down each day’s action and how he felt, and sharing his wins with a friend
Checking his progress once at the end of the year
Not tracking at all, so he doesn’t feel pressure

quiz_questions.explanation: Writing progress down and sharing it with others makes people more likely to reach their goals, just as Tara’s journal helped her.

quiz_questions.question_text: Nikhil’s flatmate left the kitchen lights on all night. Nikhil says, “You are so careless.” What kind of statement is this?

options.text: A statement of reality
Feedback
A judgment: an interpretation stated as a fact
A request

quiz_questions.explanation: “The lights were on all night” is reality. “You are careless” is Nikhil’s interpretation, stated as if it were true about the whole person.

quiz_questions.question_text: Kavya’s teammate keeps checking his phone during their project meetings. Which of these is feedback rather than a judgment?

options.text: “I noticed you checked your phone a few times today, and I felt we lost focus. Could we keep phones away for the first half hour?”
“You are so rude.”
“You never care about this project.”
“You are the worst teammate.”

quiz_questions.explanation: It describes a specific action, its impact and a feeling, and ends with a request. It does not label the person.

quiz_questions.question_text: Anil’s younger sister borrowed his bicycle and returned it with a flat tyre. Which response is a complaint rather than criticism?

options.text: “You never take care of anything.”
“What is wrong with you?”
“You are so selfish.”
“The tyre was flat when you returned the bicycle, and I was late for class. Please tell me next time something goes wrong.”

quiz_questions.explanation: A complaint names one specific issue and its effect. Criticism attacks the person’s character.

quiz_questions.question_text: A manager tells a new employee, “You are slower than everyone else on this team.” The employee’s work gets worse over the next month. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The feedback was given too quickly
The comment compared her with others and pulled her attention away from the task, towards herself
She did not hear the comment properly
Feedback never helps anyone

quiz_questions.explanation: Feedback that sounds like a verdict on the person, or compares them with others, tends to shift attention away from improving the work.

quiz_questions.question_text: Divya wants to give feedback to a friend who keeps arriving late for their weekend walks. Which word or phrase is the best way to begin?

options.text: “You always…”
“You never…”
“I noticed…”
“Why can’t you…”

quiz_questions.explanation: Feedback usually starts with “I”, such as “I notice” or “I feel”. Judgments usually start with “You”.

quiz_questions.question_text: Two classmates see a student arrive late to an important lecture. One thinks, “So lazy.” The other thinks, “Maybe the bus was delayed.” Why do they react so differently?

options.text: One of them did not see the student arrive
The student told one of them the reason
Their different beliefs led them to interpret the same event differently
Lateness is always a sign of laziness

quiz_questions.explanation: The reality was the same. Their beliefs shaped their interpretations and their emotions.

quiz_questions.question_text: Jaya’s colleague is going through a divorce and has missed two deadlines. Jaya understands why, but the missed deadlines are hurting the team. Which response shows empathy?

options.text: “I know things are hard for you right now. Can we talk about how to manage the next deadline together?”
Saying nothing and doing all of the colleague’s work herself, without asking
Telling the manager that the colleague is unreliable
Agreeing that deadlines do not matter

quiz_questions.explanation: Empathy means understanding the person’s situation. It does not mean ignoring the problem or giving up our own limits.

quiz_questions.question_text: Before a volunteering visit to an old-age home, a college class is asked to write about a day in the life of an elderly resident, imagining it from the resident’s point of view. What is this most likely to do?

options.text: Make no difference to how they see the residents
Make the students more nervous about the visit
Make them feel sorry for the residents and keep their distance
Help them see the residents with fewer stereotypes and feel more connected to them

quiz_questions.explanation: Imagining a day from another person’s point of view reduces stereotyping and helps people see what they have in common with others.

quiz_questions.question_text: Mohit’s friend snaps at him the evening before a big exam. Which is the most empathetic response?

options.text: Snapping back
Thinking, “He might be stressed about the exam,” and asking if he is okay
Deciding the friend is rude and avoiding him
Telling other friends what happened

quiz_questions.explanation: Pausing to consider the other person’s story, and asking, turns a possible conflict into support.

quiz_questions.question_text: When Asif forgets a friend’s birthday, he says, “I was so busy at work.” When the same friend forgets his birthday, Asif thinks, “He doesn’t care about me.” What is Asif doing?

options.text: Explaining his own mistake by his situation, but his friend’s by his character
Showing empathy to his friend
Giving his friend feedback
Separating reality from interpretation

quiz_questions.explanation: We often excuse our own mistakes by our situation and blame others’ mistakes on their character. Noticing this helps us be fairer. Key terms Term Meaning Neuroplasticity The brain’s ability to change and form new connections throughout life Neuron A nerve cell that passes signals to other nerve cells Grey matter Brain tissue made up mostly of the bodies of nerve cells Hippocampus A part of the brain important for memory and finding our way Amygdala A part of the brain that senses danger and sets off the stress response (the “fire alarm”) Prefrontal cortex The front part of the brain that helps us think, plan and stay calm (the “smart planner”) Cortisol A hormone the body releases when we are stressed Growth mindset The belief that we can improve our abilities through effort, good strategies and help from others Fixed mindset The belief that our abilities are set and cannot really change

quiz_questions.question_text: Ashok has been learning the tabla for a week. His fingers feel clumsy and the rhythms keep going wrong. What is happening in his brain?

options.text: Neurons are forming new connections, which will grow stronger with practice
His brain is losing old memories to make space
Nothing; his brain is not suited to music
Only children’s brains can learn music

quiz_questions.explanation: Learning creates new connections between neurons, and practice makes them stronger.

quiz_questions.question_text: Divya keeps getting chemistry problems wrong and wants to give up. Which thought is most helpful?

options.text: “Some people are just born good at chemistry.”
“I should only study subjects that come easily.”
“Cramming the night before will fix this.”
“This struggle means my brain is building new connections. If I keep practising, it will get easier.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Struggle is part of learning, and regular practice strengthens the brain’s connections.

quiz_questions.question_text: Farhan learned to type fast in college. He then stopped using a computer for a year and is now slower. What best explains this?

options.text: He has lost the skill forever
Connections that are not used weaken, but practice can strengthen them again
Typing speed is fixed at birth
His brain has stopped being able to learn

quiz_questions.explanation: Like a path through a field, a skill fades when it is not used, and practice brings it back.

quiz_questions.question_text: Meenal wants to learn Spanish before a trip in three months. Which plan best fits how the brain learns?

options.text: Studying for ten hours on the last weekend before the trip
Only revising words she already knows
Practising for 20 minutes most days, including words and phrases that are a little hard for her
Waiting until she feels naturally talented at languages

quiz_questions.explanation: Regular practice over days, on things just beyond our current level, builds strong connections.

quiz_questions.question_text: Shanti, aged 52, says, “I’m too old to learn to use a smartphone.” Based on this reading, what is the most accurate reply?

options.text: “You’re right; the brain stops changing after school.”
“Only people who are good with technology can learn it.”
“You should ask someone else to do it for you.”
“The brain keeps building new connections throughout life. With patience and daily practice, you can learn it.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity continues throughout life. Early frustration is what learning feels like at the start.

quiz_questions.question_text: Prakash did badly in a job interview. Which thought is most likely to help him learn from it?

options.text: “What went wrong, and what is one thing I will do differently next time?”
“I am a failure.”
“Interviews are unfair.”
“I will not think about it again.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Reflecting on the event, not judging himself, turns failure into a lesson.

quiz_questions.question_text: Lata’s team lost a debate competition. Which statement separates the failure from the person?

options.text: “We are hopeless at debating.”
“Our arguments on the second topic were weak, so we lost.”
“I’m just not a clever person.”
“We should never enter a competition again.”

quiz_questions.explanation: It describes what happened, not who they are. “We are hopeless” turns an event into a judgment about the self.

quiz_questions.question_text: Gaurav finds it painful to think about his own failed exam, but he can easily see what his cousin did wrong in hers. What could help him learn from his own failure?

options.text: Forgetting about the exam as soon as possible
Blaming the examiner
Stepping back and looking at his failure as if it happened to someone else
Only thinking about his past successes

quiz_questions.explanation: Failure hurts, so people tend to tune out. Looking at it from a distance makes it easier to learn from.

quiz_questions.question_text: After her first cake turns out flat, Nandini wants to understand what happened. Which is the best order of reflection questions?

options.text: Who is to blame? Why am I so bad at this? Should I stop baking?
What will others think? How can I hide it? What went wrong?
What did I learn? Why me? What happened?
What happened? What went wrong? What did I learn? What is one step I will take next time?

quiz_questions.explanation: These four questions move from facts to lessons to action, without judging the person.

quiz_questions.question_text: Joseph’s small tea stall had very few customers in its first week. What is the most helpful way to see this?

options.text: A sign that he should close the stall
Proof that he is bad at business
Useful information about what to change, such as price, location or timing
Bad luck that he cannot learn anything from

quiz_questions.explanation: Failure is part of success, not its opposite. It shows us what to change next time.

quiz_questions.question_text: Sameer says, “I can’t solve these coding problems.” Which small change in words keeps the door open to learning?

options.text: “I can’t solve these coding problems, and I never will.”
“Coding is not for people like me.”
“I can’t solve these coding problems yet.”
“Nobody can solve these problems.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Adding “yet” turns a final verdict into a step on the way. It reminds us that ability can grow with effort.

quiz_questions.question_text: Komal is stuck on a work task but does not ask her senior for help, because she is sure he will say no. What does this reading suggest?

options.text: People are usually more willing to help than we expect, so it is worth asking
She is right; most people refuse to help
Asking for help is a sign of weakness
She should wait until the deadline has passed

quiz_questions.explanation: We tend to underestimate how willing others are to help, so we ask less often than we could.

quiz_questions.question_text: Tushar worries that asking his manager for advice will make him look less capable. What does this reading suggest?

options.text: Asking for advice always makes people look weak
Asking for advice on a hard task can make people look more competent, not less
He should never ask questions at work
It does not matter how others see him

quiz_questions.explanation: Asking for advice, especially on a difficult task, can make others see us as more capable.

quiz_questions.question_text: Mansi needs help with a statistics assignment. Which request is most likely to get useful help?

options.text: “Can you just do it for me?”
“I’m useless at this.”
Saying nothing and hoping someone notices
“I’ve solved the first two questions, but I’m stuck on how to find the mean in question 3. Could you show me the first step?”

quiz_questions.explanation: A clear, specific request that shows what you have already tried makes it easier for others to help.

quiz_questions.question_text: Zoya has been learning to drive for two weeks and still stalls the car often. She thinks, “I’m not a good driver.” Which thought fits a growth mindset?

options.text: “I’m not a good driver yet. With more practice and help from my instructor, I’ll improve.”
“Some people are just born good drivers.”
“I should stop learning before I embarrass myself.”
“Stalling means I will never be able to drive.”

quiz_questions.explanation: “Yet” and asking for help work together: they keep us trying and give us support while we learn.

quiz_questions.question_text: Arjun studied well for his driving test, but when the examiner sits beside him, he forgets which mirror to check first. What best explains this?

options.text: He did not study at all
His amygdala has set off the stress alarm, and his prefrontal cortex, the planner, is working less well
His memory is permanently damaged
Driving tests are physically dangerous

quiz_questions.explanation: When the amygdala gets louder, the prefrontal cortex goes quiet, so it is harder to recall what we know.

quiz_questions.question_text: Seema’s heart races before every job interview, even though nothing can physically hurt her there. Why does her body react this way?

options.text: Interviews are always dangerous
Only weak people feel stress
Her prefrontal cortex is causing the panic
The brain does not always know the difference between a real danger and a stressful situation

quiz_questions.explanation: The amygdala can react to an interview or exam as if it were a real threat.

quiz_questions.question_text: Kabir feels panic rising just before he presents to his class. Which is the quickest way to calm his body and mind?

options.text: Telling himself firmly to stop feeling nervous
Drinking two cups of strong coffee
Doing a minute of slow 4–2–4 breathing
Running out of the room

quiz_questions.explanation: We cannot just tell the amygdala to switch off, but slow breathing sends the body a signal that it is safe.

quiz_questions.question_text: Pooja wants to try the 4–2–4 breathing exercise before a meeting. Which instructions should she follow?

options.text: Breathe in for 4, hold for 2, breathe out for 4, and repeat for about a minute
Breathe in for 2, hold for 4, breathe out for 2
Breathe quickly for 4 seconds, then rest
Hold her breath for as long as possible

quiz_questions.explanation: Breathe in through the nose for 4 counts, hold gently for 2, and breathe out through the mouth for 4. Repeating this for about a minute slows the breathing to around six breaths a minute.

quiz_questions.question_text: Waseem’s manager keeps changing his deadlines without warning, and Waseem finds it hard to think clearly at work. What does this reading suggest?

options.text: Stress that feels out of our control can quickly weaken clear thinking, and short breathing breaks may help
He is simply not clever enough for the job
Stress always improves performance
Nothing can be done about stress

quiz_questions.explanation: Stress we cannot control weakens the thinking part of the brain. Regular slow breathing can help us calm down and focus.

quiz_questions.question_text: Sahana is not selected for her college debate team. Which response best shows a growth mindset?

options.text: “I’m just not a good speaker.”
“I’ll ask the coach what to work on and keep practising for next time.”
“The selectors were unfair.”
“I’ll never try out again.”

quiz_questions.explanation: She treats the result as information, asks for help and keeps improving.

quiz_questions.question_text: Before his exam results come out, Nitin says, “If I pass, I’ll keep studying. If I don’t, I’ll still keep studying.” What does this show?

options.text: He does not care about his results
He is sure he has failed
He is calm about the result and committed to the process, which he can control
He has given up

quiz_questions.explanation: A growth mindset focuses on effort and learning, which we can control, rather than outcomes we cannot.

quiz_questions.question_text: Aditi studies the same way for twice as many hours, but her marks do not improve. What would a growth mindset suggest?

options.text: “Effort alone guarantees success, so I’ll study even longer.”
“I’m just not smart enough.”
“Marks don’t matter.”
“Let me try a different way of studying and ask my teacher for feedback.”

quiz_questions.explanation: Effort works best with good strategies, feedback and help from others. Working longer in the same unhelpful way is not the same as growing.

quiz_questions.question_text: Kunal’s colleague wins an award, and Kunal thinks, “She’s just naturally gifted.” Which is the growth mindset version of this thought?

options.text: “What did she do to get that good?”
“I’ll never be as good as her.”
“She was lucky.”
“Awards don’t mean anything.”

quiz_questions.explanation: A growth mindset turns comparison into curiosity about the effort and strategies behind success.

quiz_questions.question_text: A school runs a one-hour growth mindset session for its students. What is a realistic expectation?

options.text: Every student’s grades will rise sharply
It may help some students, especially those who are struggling, but it works best alongside good teaching, practice and support
It will have no effect on anyone
Students will no longer need teachers

quiz_questions.explanation: A growth mindset is helpful, but it is not magic. It works best with the other habits and support covered in this module.
